claim: Activin A belongs to the TGFβ/BMP family of ligands.
source: Activin A is a protein that belongs to the TGFß/BMP family of ligands (Hinck et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Hinck et al., 2016.

claim: TGFβ/BMP ligands initiate signaling by driving the formation of heterotetrameric complexes of their cognate type I and type II receptors.
source: These ligands initiate signaling by driving the formation of heterotetrameric complexes of their cognate type I and type II receptors, and where a dimeric ligand brings together two type I and two type II receptors (Yadin et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Yadin et al., 2016.

claim: A dimeric ligand brings together two type I and two type II receptors.
source: These ligands initiate signaling by driving the formation of heterotetrameric complexes of their cognate type I and type II receptors, and where a dimeric ligand brings together two type I and two type II receptors (Yadin et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Yadin et al., 2016.

claim: There are seven type I receptors that mediate signaling for the TGFβ/BMP family of ligands.
source: There are seven type I and five type II receptors that mediate signaling for this family of ligands.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: There are five type II receptors that mediate signaling for the TGFβ/BMP family of ligands.
source: There are seven type I and five type II receptors that mediate signaling for this family of ligands.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: The choice of type I receptor in the signaling complex is the main determinant of which of two signaling pathways is activated.
source: The choice of type I receptor in the signaling complex is the main determinant of which of two signaling pathways is activated: Smad1/5/8, when the type I receptors are ACVRL1, ACVR1, BMPR1A, or BMPR1B; and Smad2/3, when the type I receptors are ACVR1B, TGFBR1, or ACVR1C.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: Smad1/5/8 signaling is activated when the type I receptors are ACVRL1, ACVR1, BMPR1A, or BMPR1B.
source: The choice of type I receptor in the signaling complex is the main determinant of which of two signaling pathways is activated: Smad1/5/8, when the type I receptors are ACVRL1, ACVR1, BMPR1A, or BMPR1B; and Smad2/3, when the type I receptors are ACVR1B, TGFBR1, or ACVR1C.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: Smad2/3 signaling is activated when the type I receptors are ACVR1B, TGFBR1, or ACVR1C.
source: The choice of type I receptor in the signaling complex is the main determinant of which of two signaling pathways is activated: Smad1/5/8, when the type I receptors are ACVRL1, ACVR1, BMPR1A, or BMPR1B; and Smad2/3, when the type I receptors are ACVR1B, TGFBR1, or ACVR1C.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: Activin A utilizes ACVR1B as its type I receptor in conjunction with the type II receptors ACVR2A, ACVR2B, and, to a lesser extent, BMPR2 to signal through Smad2/3.
source: Activin A utilizes ACVR1B as its type I receptor in conjunction with the type II receptors ACVR2A, ACVR2B, and, to a lesser extent, BMPR2 to signal through Smad2/3 (Aykul et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Aykul et al., 2017.

claim: The biological functions of Activin A have been investigated widely using multiple approaches.
source: The biological functions of Activin A have been investigated widely using multiple approaches (Makanji et al., 2014; Namwanje and Brown, 2016) including reverse genetics experiments wherein the gene encoding for Activin A – Inhba – has been 'knocked out' (Archambeault and Yao, 2010; Matzuk et al., 1995; Pangas et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Makanji et al., 2014 and Namwanje and Brown, 2016.

claim: Reverse genetics experiments have been used to investigate the biological functions of Activin A by knocking out the gene encoding for Activin A (Inhba).
source: The biological functions of Activin A have been investigated widely using multiple approaches (Makanji et al., 2014; Namwanje and Brown, 2016) including reverse genetics experiments wherein the gene encoding for Activin A – Inhba – has been 'knocked out' (Archambeault and Yao, 2010; Matzuk et al., 1995; Pangas et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Archambeault and Yao, 2010; Matzuk et al., 1995; Pangas et al., 2007.

claim: The results of Inhba knockout experiments have been largely interpreted in the context of Activin A acting as an agonist of ACVR1B to induce Smad2/3 or other signaling pathways.
source: The results of those experiments have been largely interpreted in the context of Activin A acting as an agonist of ACVR1B to induce Smad2/3 or other signaling pathways (Archambeault and Yao, 2010; Makanji et al., 2014; Namwanje and Brown, 2016; Pangas et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Archambeault and Yao, 2010; Makanji et al., 2014; Namwanje and Brown, 2016; Pangas et al., 2007.

claim: ACVR1 was originally cloned as the type I receptor for Activin A.
source: Interestingly, ACVR1 was originally cloned as the type I receptor for Activin A (Attisano et al., 1993; Tsuchida et al., 1993), but the inability of Activin A to activate ACVR1, followed by the discovery that BMP7 activates it, led to a 'relabeling' of ACVR1 as a BMP receptor (Macías-Silva et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Attisano et al., 1993 and Tsuchida et al., 1993.

claim: The inability of Activin A to activate ACVR1, followed by the discovery that BMP7 activates it, led to a 'relabeling' of ACVR1 as a BMP receptor.
source: Interestingly, ACVR1 was originally cloned as the type I receptor for Activin A (Attisano et al., 1993; Tsuchida et al., 1993), but the inability of Activin A to activate ACVR1, followed by the discovery that BMP7 activates it, led to a 'relabeling' of ACVR1 as a BMP receptor (Macías-Silva et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Macías-Silva et al., 1998.

claim: Activin A can engage the type I receptor ACVR1 to form an ACVR1•Activin A•type II receptor non-signaling complex (NSC).
source: However, recent studies pinpoint a previously unrecognized property of Activin A: that it can engage the type I receptor ACVR1, to form an ACVR1•Activin A•type II receptor non-signaling complex (NSC) (Hatsell et al., 2015; Olsen et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Hatsell et al., 2015 and Olsen et al., 2015.

claim: The NSC is unique in that its stoichiometry is identical to that of corresponding signaling complexes formed between the same receptors and BMPs.
source: This NSC is unique in that its stoichiometry is identical to that of corresponding signaling complexes formed between the same receptors and BMPs, but also in that it is converted into a signaling complex in the ACVR1-driven genetic disorder fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: The NSC is converted into a signaling complex in the ACVR1-driven genetic disorder fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP).
source: This NSC is unique in that its stoichiometry is identical to that of corresponding signaling complexes formed between the same receptors and BMPs, but also in that it is converted into a signaling complex in the ACVR1-driven genetic disorder fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: The NSC functions to tie down Activin A and render it unavailable for signaling.
source: Excluding the special situation of FOP (see below), the NSC functions to tie down Activin A and render it unavailable for signaling, but also to tie down the type II receptors and ACVR1 and render them unavailable for engagement with BMPs, hence resulting in an apparent inhibition of ACVR1-mediated BMP signaling; in cells where ACVR1 is the main type I receptor, Activin A inhibits BMP6- (Hatsell et al., 2015) and BMP7-induced signaling (this work).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: The NSC functions to tie down the type II receptors and ACVR1 and render them unavailable for engagement with BMPs.
source: Excluding the special situation of FOP (see below), the NSC functions to tie down Activin A and render it unavailable for signaling, but also to tie down the type II receptors and ACVR1 and render them unavailable for engagement with BMPs, hence resulting in an apparent inhibition of ACVR1-mediated BMP signaling; in cells where ACVR1 is the main type I receptor, Activin A inhibits BMP6- (Hatsell et al., 2015) and BMP7-induced signaling (this work).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: The NSC results in an apparent inhibition of ACVR1-mediated BMP signaling.
source: Excluding the special situation of FOP (see below), the NSC functions to tie down Activin A and render it unavailable for signaling, but also to tie down the type II receptors and ACVR1 and render them unavailable for engagement with BMPs, hence resulting in an apparent inhibition of ACVR1-mediated BMP signaling; in cells where ACVR1 is the main type I receptor, Activin A inhibits BMP6- (Hatsell et al., 2015) and BMP7-induced signaling (this work).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: In cells where ACVR1 is the main type I receptor, Activin A inhibits BMP6-induced signaling.
source: Excluding the special situation of FOP (see below), the NSC functions to tie down Activin A and render it unavailable for signaling, but also to tie down the type II receptors and ACVR1 and render them unavailable for engagement with BMPs, hence resulting in an apparent inhibition of ACVR1-mediated BMP signaling; in cells where ACVR1 is the main type I receptor, Activin A inhibits BMP6- (Hatsell et al., 2015) and BMP7-induced signaling (this work).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Hatsell et al., 2015.

claim: In cells where ACVR1 is the main type I receptor, Activin A inhibits BMP7-induced signaling.
source: Excluding the special situation of FOP (see below), the NSC functions to tie down Activin A and render it unavailable for signaling, but also to tie down the type II receptors and ACVR1 and render them unavailable for engagement with BMPs, hence resulting in an apparent inhibition of ACVR1-mediated BMP signaling; in cells where ACVR1 is the main type I receptor, Activin A inhibits BMP6- (Hatsell et al., 2015) and BMP7-induced signaling (this work).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data presented in this work.

claim: FOP is a rare autosomal-dominant genetic disorder.
source: FOP is a rare autosomal-dominant genetic disorder that arises from missense mutations in the sequence encoding the intracellular domain of ACVR1 (Katagiri et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Katagiri et al., 2018.

claim: FOP arises from missense mutations in the sequence encoding the intracellular domain of ACVR1.
source: FOP is a rare autosomal-dominant genetic disorder that arises from missense mutations in the sequence encoding the intracellular domain of ACVR1 (Katagiri et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Katagiri et al., 2018.

claim: The most clinically important feature of FOP is the episodic, yet progressive and cumulative, formation of heterotopic bone in connective tissue.
source: The most clinically important feature of FOP is the episodic, yet progressive and cumulative, formation of heterotopic bone in connective tissue, a process referred to as heterotopic ossification (HO) (Hüning and Gillessen-Kaesbach, 2014).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Hüning and Gillessen-Kaesbach, 2014.

claim: FOP-mutant variants of ACVR1 display the neomorphic property of recognizing Activin A as an agonistic ligand.
source: FOP-mutant variants of ACVR1 display the neomorphic property of recognizing Activin A (as well as other Activins) as an agonistic ligand, much like a BMP (Hatsell et al., 2015; Hino et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Hatsell et al., 2015 and Hino et al., 2015.

claim: FOP-mutant variants of ACVR1 recognize other Activins as agonistic ligands.
source: FOP-mutant variants of ACVR1 display the neomorphic property of recognizing Activin A (as well as other Activins) as an agonistic ligand, much like a BMP (Hatsell et al., 2015; Hino et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Hatsell et al., 2015 and Hino et al., 2015.

claim: In mouse FOP, activation of FOP-mutant ACVR1 by Activin A is required for HO.
source: In mouse FOP, activation of FOP-mutant ACVR1 by Activin A is required for HO, as demonstrated by experiments where inhibition of Activin A, using highly specific monoclonal antibodies, halts both the occurrence and the progression of HO (Hatsell et al., 2015; Lees-Shepard et al., 2018a; Lees-Shepard et al., 2018b; Upadhyay et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Hatsell et al., 2015; Lees-Shepard et al., 2018a; Lees-Shepard et al., 2018b; Upadhyay et al., 2017.

claim: Inhibition of Activin A using highly specific monoclonal antibodies halts both the occurrence and the progression of HO in mouse FOP.
source: In mouse FOP, activation of FOP-mutant ACVR1 by Activin A is required for HO, as demonstrated by experiments where inhibition of Activin A, using highly specific monoclonal antibodies, halts both the occurrence and the progression of HO (Hatsell et al., 2015; Lees-Shepard et al., 2018a; Lees-Shepard et al., 2018b; Upadhyay et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Hatsell et al., 2015; Lees-Shepard et al., 2018a; Lees-Shepard et al., 2018b; Upadhyay et al., 2017.

claim: In FOP, the ACVR1[FOP mutant]•Activin A•type II receptor complex acts as a signaling complex.
source: Thus, in FOP, the ACVR1[FOP mutant]•Activin A•type II receptor complex, which is stoichiometrically identical to the NSC, acts as a signaling complex.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: FOP is autosomal-dominant, so one wild-type copy of ACVR1 remains operational.
source: However, since FOP is autosomal-dominant, one wild-type copy of ACVR1 remains operational and hence capable of sequestering Activin A in NSCs.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: Wild-type ACVR1 is capable of sequestering Activin A in NSCs.
source: However, since FOP is autosomal-dominant, one wild-type copy of ACVR1 remains operational and hence capable of sequestering Activin A in NSCs.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: In mouse FOP, removal of the wild-type copy of Acvr1 exacerbates the degree of HO.
source: In mouse FOP, removal of the wild-type copy of Acvr1 exacerbates the degree of HO (Lees-Shepard et al., 2018b).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Lees-Shepard et al., 2018b.

claim: Loss of wild-type ACVR1 results in loss of the NSC and concomitant increase in the number of active complexes between Activin A and FOP-mutant ACVR1.
source: These data are consistent with a model where loss of wild-type ACVR1 results in loss of the NSC and concomitant increase in the number of active complexes between Activin A and FOP-mutant ACVR1.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as a model consistent with the data.

claim: In myeloma cells in culture, Activin A protects them from BMP9-induced apoptosis.
source: Outside of FOP, exploration of the NSC has been limited to myeloma cells in culture, wherein Activin A protects them from BMP9-induced apoptosis (Olsen et al., 2015); whether a similar phenomenon takes place in vivo is currently unknown.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Olsen et al., 2015.

claim: The authors engineered a set of 'agonist-only' Activin A muteins that retain their ability to activate ACVR1B but fail to form the NSC with ACVR1.
source: In order to begin to address such knowledge gaps, we engineered a set of 'agonist-only' Activin A muteins that retain their ability to activate ACVR1B but fail to form the NSC with ACVR1.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The finger two tip loop (F2TL) region of Activin A is critical for the formation of the NSC.
source: Using these muteins, we show that the finger two tip loop (F2TL) region of Activin A is critical for the formation of the NSC, and we obtain conclusive in vivo evidence that the NSC is required for tempering the degree of HO in mouse FOP.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The NSC is required for tempering the degree of HO in mouse FOP.
source: Using these muteins, we show that the finger two tip loop (F2TL) region of Activin A is critical for the formation of the NSC, and we obtain conclusive in vivo evidence that the NSC is required for tempering the degree of HO in mouse FOP.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SD208 inhibits TGFβ1-induced Smad2/3 signaling with an IC50 of 1.4 nM.
source: (top panel) SD208 (TFGBR1 kinase inhibitor) inhibits Activin A-induced Smad2/3 signaling (IC50: 3.2 nM) and TGFβ1-induced Smad2/3 signaling (IC50: 1.4 nM) but does not affect BMP6-induced Smad1/5/8/signaling.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: SD208 does not affect BMP6-induced Smad1/5/8 signaling.
source: (top panel) SD208 (TFGBR1 kinase inhibitor) inhibits Activin A-induced Smad2/3 signaling (IC50: 3.2 nM) and TGFβ1-induced Smad2/3 signaling (IC50: 1.4 nM) but does not affect BMP6-induced Smad1/5/8/signaling.

claim: MAB222 leaves TGFβ1-induced Smad2/3 signaling unaffected.

evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

source: (bottom panel) MAB222 (ACVR1B neutralizing antibody) inhibits Activin A induced Smad2/3 signaling (IC50: 37.4 nM) but leaves TGFβ1-induced Smad2/3 and BMP6-induced Smad1/5/8 signaling unaffected.

claim: MAB222 plus SD208 inhibit Activin A-induced Smad2/3 phosphorylation but not BMP6-induced Smad1/5/8 phosphorylation.

claim: Activin A does not induce Smad1/5/8 phosphorylation via wild-type ACVR1.
source: Consistent with prior observations, Activin A does not induce Smad1/5/8 phosphorylation via wild-type ACVR1.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The Activin A•ACVR1•type II receptor complex does not directly activate downstream signaling of the pathways included in the Human Phosphokinase Array.
source: The Activin A•ACVR1•type II receptor complex does not directly activate downstream signaling of the pathways included in this panel, as evidenced by the lack of increases in any of the phosphoproteins assayed therein.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: Treatment of ACVR1-expressing cells with Activin A does not result in phosphorylation of a set of proteins that represent major signaling pathways activated by receptor kinases.
source: Comparison of the 37 proteins whose phosphorylation state can be interrogated using this array reveals of that there is no induction of phosphorylation by Activin A.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: The only significant differences detected in the Human Phosphokinase Array were minor reductions in the phosphorylation level of STAT3 (S727) and STAT5.
source: The only significant differences detected were minor reductions in the phosphorylation level of STAT3 (S727) and STAT5 (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: Engagement of ACVR1 by Activin A suppresses signaling.
source: These results are consistent with the idea that the ACVR1•Activin A•type II receptor complex acts as an NSC: it does not transduce signal either through the Smads or any of the other proteins interrogated here – if anything, engagement of ACVR1 by Activin A suppresses signaling.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Treatment of mES cells with Activin A in the presence of SD208 does not result in any increases in phosphorylation in the proteins interrogated by the Human Phosphokinase Array.
source: Consistent with the results shown in Figure 1, treatment of mES cells with Activin A in the presence of SD208 does not result in any increases in phosphorylation in the proteins interrogated by this array (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Activin A.Nod.F2TL exhibited activity very close to that of wild-type Activin A in activating Smad2/3 signaling.
source: Of these three muteins, the Activin A.Nod.F2TL exhibited activity very close to that of wild-type Activin A (Figure 4), whereas the other two were less active (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Activin A.Nod.pre and Activin A.Nod.post were less active than wild-type Activin A in activating Smad2/3 signaling.
source: Of these three muteins, the Activin A.Nod.F2TL exhibited activity very close to that of wild-type Activin A (Figure 4), whereas the other two were less active (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nodal lacks an aspartic acid at position 406.
source: This comparison revealed an intriguing difference between the fingertips of these ligands: that Nodal lacks an aspartic acid at position 406 (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The aspartic acid at position 406 in Activin A is highly conserved across different species.
source: Moreover, an alignment of Activin A from different species reveals that this residue is highly conserved (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), whereas it varies when the different Activins are compared (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Activin A.∆D406 exhibits identical activity to wild type Activin A in activating ACVR1B.
source: As shown on Figure 4A, Activin A.Nod.F2TL is slightly less active than Activin A, whereas Activin A.∆D406 exhibits identical activity to wild type Activin A, making Activin A.∆D406 a second potential candidate for an agonist-only Activin A variant to study further.

claim: Both Activin A.Nod.F2TL and Activin A.∆D406 are identical to Activin A in their ability to dimerize ACVR1B and TGFBR1 along with the corresponding type II receptors.
source: In line with our bioassay results, both Activin A.Nod.F2TL and Activin A.∆D406 are identical to Activin A in their ability to dimerize ACVR1B and TGFBR1 along with the corresponding type II receptors (Figure 4B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: Activin A can engage ACVR1 into a complex with type II receptors, but that complex is not stable enough to be isolated in vitro.

claim: Crosslinking is required to detect binding of Activin A to ACVR1.
source: This is in line with prior observations that crosslinking is required to detect binding of Activin A to ACVR1 (Attisano et al., 1993; Piek et al., 1999; Tsuchida et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Attisano et al., 1993; Piek et al., 1999; Tsuchida et al., 1993.

claim: Activin A.Nod.F2TL is approximately 60-fold less effective at inhibiting BMP7 than wild-type Activin A.

evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Activin A.∆D406 is approximately 15-fold less effective at inhibiting BMP7 than wild-type Activin A.
source: In contrast, both Activin A.Nod.F2TL and Activin A.∆D406 were approximately 60-fold and 15-fold less effective at inhibiting BMP7, respectively (Figure 5; Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Both Activin A.Nod.F2TL and Activin A.∆D406 display greatly reduced ability to induce dimerization of ACVR1 with ACVR2A.

evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: REGN2476 completely alleviates inhibition of BMP7 signaling by Activin A.Nod.F2TL.

evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The remaining inhibition of BMP7 signaling by Activin A.Nod.F2TL is a result of binding of this mutein to type II receptors.
source: Furthermore, REGN2476, an anti-Activin A monoclonal antibody that neutralizes Activin A by blocking its binding to its type II receptors (Figure 5—figure supplement 5), completely alleviates inhibition of BMP7 signaling by Activin A.Nod.F2TL further indicating that the remaining inhibition is a result of binding of this mutein to type II receptors (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: H4H10442 shifts the dose response of the inhibition brought about by wild-type Activin A on BMP7-initiated signaling to that obtained by Activin A.Nod.F2TL.

evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The reduced inhibition obtained with Activin A.Nod.F2TL is a direct consequence of the inability of Activin A.Nod.F2TL's F2TL region to bind ACVR1.
source: Indeed, H4H10442 shifts the dose response of the inhibition brought about by wild-type Activin A on BMP7-initiated signaling to that obtained by Activin A.Nod.F2TL (Figure 5B), hence verifying that the reduced inhibition obtained with Activin A.Nod.F2TL is a direct consequence of the inability of Activin A.Nod.F2TL's F2TL region (which is that of Nodal) to bind ACVR1.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Activin A.∆D406 has partially retained the ability to antagonize BMP7 signaling via ACVR1.

claim: The ACVR1•Activin A•type II receptor complex does not transduce signal by utilizing signaling proteins other than Smad1/5/8.
source: Therefore, in order to exclude the possibility that the ACVR1•Activin A•type II receptor may transduce signal by utilizing signaling proteins other than Smad1/5/8, we examined whether treatment of ACVR1-expressing cells with Activin A would result in phosphorylation of a set of proteins that represent major signaling pathways activated by receptor kinases.

claim: D406 extends into the type I binding site and is flanked by two lysine residues from ACVR1.
